A shopkeeper buys 25 double-rotis at Rs 10 each and sells at Rs 13 each, but 7 rotis got spoiled. The result is:
A person buys 10 dozen eggs at Rs 120 per dozen; 3 dozen break; the rest sell at Rs 130 per dozen. The result is:
A bookseller buys 20 maths books at Rs 120 each and sells them at Rs 125 each. His percent profit is:
mcqs.why: Profit per book = 125 − 120 = 5. Profit % = (5/120) × 100% = 4 1/6% profit. (The number of books does not change the percent.)

mcqs.q: A shopkeeper bears a loss on a jacket with CP Rs 1,000; the loss is Rs 150. The percent loss is:
At a 20% discount, Umeed bought a dinner set for Rs 52,000. The original price was:
mcqs.why: After a 20% discount she paid 80% of the original price. Original = 52,000 ÷ 80% = 52,000 × 100/80 = Rs 65,000.

mcqs.q: A ladies' purse has original price Rs 1,500 and is sold at a 15% discount (Exercise 7.3, Q6 pattern). The selling price is:
mcqs.why: Discount = 15% of 1,500 = 225. Selling price = 1,500 − 225 = Rs 1,275.

mcqs.q: Profit percent is always calculated on:
mcqs.why: By definition, profit % and loss % are calculated on the COST price: (profit ÷ CP) × 100%.

mcqs.q: If SP > CP, then there is:
mcqs.why: When the selling price is greater than the cost price, the seller gains — that gain is called profit, equal to SP − CP.

mcqs.q: After a discount of 2 1/2%, the percent of the price actually paid is:
mcqs.why: Percent paid = 100% − discount% = 100% − 2 1/2% = 97 1/2%. This is the rate used in Review Exercise 7, Q5 to recover a car's original price.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 7 — Financial Arithmetic: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Percent = out of 100. Convert: percent ↔ fraction (over 100) ↔ decimal (÷ or × 100).
  • Percent of a quantity = (percent/100) × quantity; part as percent = (part/total) × 100%.
  • Profit = SP − CP; loss = CP − SP; percents always on CP.
  • Discount percent is calculated on the original (marked) price.
  • Compare two performances by converting both to percents.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 7, Q2)

A colour TV's previous price was Rs 17,400; it is now available for Rs 13,050. Find the percent discount.

Step 1: Discount = 17,400 − 13,050 = Rs 4,350.

Step 2: Discount % = (4,350/17,400) × 100% = 25%.

Answer: 25% discount.

mcqs.q: Karim bought 50 dozen pencils at Rs 60 per dozen and sold them all at Rs 13 per pencil. His percent profit is:
Imran obtained 548/800 and another student 459/600. Whose performance is better?
mcqs.why: Imran: 548/800 × 100% = 68.5%. Other student: 459/600 × 100% = 76.5%. Since 76.5% > 68.5%, the other student's performance is better — compare percents, not raw marks, when totals differ.

mcqs.q: A fruit seller buys 50 dozen bananas at Rs 60 per dozen; 10 dozen go bad; the rest sell at Rs 70 per dozen. The result is:
A car was sold for Rs 87,500 after a 2 1/2% discount (Review Q5). The price actually paid was what percent of the original?
mcqs.why: Percent paid = 100% − 2 1/2% = 97 1/2%. The original price = 87,500 ÷ 97 1/2%, about Rs 89,743.59.

mcqs.q: 75% as a decimal is:
mcqs.why: To write a percent as a decimal, divide by 100: 75 ÷ 100 = 0.75. So 75% and 0.75 are the same value in two forms.

mcqs.q: 3/5 as a percent is:
mcqs.why: To change a fraction into a percent, multiply by 100%: 3/5 × 100% = 300/5 % = 60%. So 3/5 = 60%.

mcqs.q: 20% of Rs 450 is:
mcqs.why: 20% of Rs 450 = 20/100 × 450 = Rs 90. First find 1% (450 ÷ 100 = 4.5) or use the formula directly — either way the part is Rs 90.

mcqs.q: An item with CP Rs 200 is sold for Rs 170. The percent loss is:
Discount percent is calculated on:
mcqs.why: Discount % = (discount ÷ original price) × 100% — as in the TV example: 4,350/17,400 = 25%.

mcqs.q: Which is the correct order to find percent profit?
mcqs.why: Profit percent = (profit ÷ cost price) × 100%. The base is always the cost price.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.1 — Writing Sentences in Symbols; Open Statements
lessons.notes_html:
Algebra uses letters for numbers

A letter like x, y or z stands for a number we may not know yet — it is called a variable. Sentences in words are written in symbols: "a number x added to 4" → x + 4; "a number y multiplied by seven" → 7y (the × sign is dropped).

Statements: true, false, open

A statement with only numbers is either true or false (8 + 3 = 11 is true; 5 + 9 = 18 is false). A statement containing a variable, like D + 3 = 9, is an open statement — it becomes true only for the right value of the variable.

Worked example (from Exercise 8.1, Q4)

Find the value of Δ that makes 6 + Δ = 15 true.

Step 1: Δ is the missing part: Δ = 15 − 6.

Step 2: Δ = 9.

Step 3: Check: 6 + 9 = 15 ✓.

Answer: Δ = 9

mcqs.q: 'A number x added to 4' in symbols is:
mcqs.why: 'Added to' means addition: the number x plus 4 is written x + 4.

mcqs.q: 'Six added to a number z is less than four' in symbols is:
mcqs.why: Six plus z is 6 + z, and 'is less than four' uses the sign <: 6 + z < 4.

mcqs.q: The statement 8 + 3 = 11 is:
mcqs.why: 8 + 3 really is 11, so the statement is true.

mcqs.q: The statement 18 − 13 = 15 is:
mcqs.why: 18 − 13 = 5, not 15, so the statement is false.

mcqs.q: D + 3 = 9 is an open statement because:
options: D is a variable whose value is not fixed
mcqs.why: An open statement contains a variable whose value is not yet fixed. D + 3 = 9 is true only when D = 6.

mcqs.q: The value of □ in □ + 5 = 8 is:
mcqs.why: The missing number is found by subtracting: □ = 8 − 5 = 3. Check by putting it back: 3 + 5 = 8 ✓, so □ = 3 makes the open statement true.

mcqs.q: 'A number y multiplied by seven' is written:
mcqs.why: In algebra the multiplication sign is dropped between a number and a variable: 7 × y is written 7y.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an open statement?
mcqs.why: 3a + 4 = 8 contains the variable a, whose value is not fixed, so it is an open statement. The others contain only numbers and are simply true.

mcqs.q: The value of Δ in 6 + Δ = 15 is:
mcqs.why: Δ is the part that must be added to 6 to make 15: Δ = 15 − 6 = 9. Check: 6 + 9 = 15 ✓. Finding such a value is the first step towards solving equations.

mcqs.q: 'The price of x books at 18 rupees per book' in symbols (Review pattern) is:
mcqs.why: Total price = price of one book × number of books = 18 × x = 18x rupees.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.2 — Terms, Variables, Constants, Coefficients and Like Terms
lessons.notes_html:
Parts of an expression

  • Terms are the parts of an expression separated by + or −. 4ℓ + 3m + 9 has 3 terms.
  • A variable is a letter standing for a changing number (x in 8x + 3).
  • A constant term is a term with no variable (the 2 in 2x + 2).
  • The numerical coefficient is the number multiplying the variable (−7 in −7x).
  • Like terms have exactly the same variables: 2xy, 140xy, 5xy are like terms; −7xz and xz are like terms.

Worked example (from Exercise 8.2, Q5)

From 2xy, 4ℓm, −7xz, 140xy, 13mn, xz, 5xy, −2p, 46p — pick the like terms.

Step 1: Group by the variable part: xy-terms: 2xy, 140xy, 5xy.

Step 2: xz-terms: −7xz, xz.

Step 3: p-terms: −2p, 46p. 4ℓm and 13mn stand alone.

Answer: Like-term groups are (2xy, 140xy, 5xy), (−7xz, xz) and (−2p, 46p).

mcqs.q: The number of terms in 3 × m × n is:
mcqs.why: Terms are separated by + or − signs only. 3 × m × n is one product with no + or −, so it is a single term.

mcqs.q: The number of terms in 4ℓ + 3m + 9 is:
mcqs.why: The + signs separate the expression into three terms: 4ℓ, 3m and 9.

mcqs.q: The variable in 8x + 3 is:
mcqs.why: The variable is the letter that can change value: x. The numbers 8 and 3 are fixed.

mcqs.q: The constant term of 2x + 2 is:
mcqs.why: A constant term has no variable attached. In 2x + 2 the term 2 is the constant term.

mcqs.q: The constant term of −3 + x is:
mcqs.why: The term without a variable is −3 (with its negative sign). So the constant term is −3.

mcqs.q: The numerical coefficient of x in −7x is:
mcqs.why: The numerical coefficient is the number multiplying the variable, including its sign: in −7x the coefficient of x is −7.

mcqs.q: The numerical coefficient in 5y is:
mcqs.why: 5y means 5 × y, so the numerical coefficient of y is 5.

mcqs.q: Which group contains only like terms?
mcqs.why: Like terms have exactly the same variable part. 2xy, 140xy and 1/5 xy all have the variable part xy, so they are like terms.

mcqs.q: −7xz and xz are:
mcqs.why: Both have the same variable part xz, so they are like terms. Coefficients (−7 and 1) may differ; that does not matter.

mcqs.q: In the expression 7x + 5 + 8, the terms are:
mcqs.why: The + signs split the expression into three terms: 7x, 5 and 8. Constants 5 and 8 are separate terms until we choose to add them.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.3 — Addition and Subtraction of Algebraic Expressions
lessons.notes_html:
Only like terms can be added or subtracted

Add or subtract the coefficients of like terms and keep the variable part unchanged:

2x + 9x = (2 + 9)x = 11x

Unlike terms (like 2b and 3a) cannot be combined — they stay as they are. When expressions have several variables, collect each kind of like term separately. In subtraction, change the signs inside the bracket being subtracted.

Worked example (from Exercise 8.3, Q3)

Add: 3a + 2b, a + b, 4a.

Step 1: Write together: (3a + 2b) + (a + b) + 4a.

Step 2: Collect a-terms: 3a + a + 4a = 8a.

Step 3: Collect b-terms: 2b + b = 3b.

Answer: 8a + 3b

mcqs.why: Add the coefficients of the like terms: 2 + 1 + 4 = 7 (remember plain x has coefficient 1). So the sum is 7x.
Coefficients: 2 + 3 + 6 + 1 = 12, so the sum is 12a.

mcqs.q: a + 2a + 3a in simplest form is:
mcqs.why: All three are like terms in a, so add their coefficients: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 (plain a has coefficient 1). Hence a + 2a + 3a = 6a.
Collect like terms: x: 6 + 2 + 2 = 10x; y: 5 + 3 + 1 = 9y; z: 7 + 1 = 8z. Sum = 10x + 9y + 8z.

mcqs.q: Subtract 5x from 8x:
mcqs.why: 8x − 5x = (8 − 5)x = 3x. 'Subtract A from B' means B − A.

mcqs.q: Subtract −3y from 9y:
mcqs.why: 9y − (−3y) = 9y + 3y = 12y. Subtracting a negative term adds its positive.

mcqs.q: Subtract (2x + 3y) from (6x + 8y):
mcqs.why: (6x + 8y) − (2x + 3y) = 6x + 8y − 2x − 3y = 4x + 5y. Every sign inside the subtracted bracket changes.

mcqs.q: 12ab − 9ab =
mcqs.why: Subtract the coefficients of the like terms: (12 − 9)ab = 3ab. (The book lists this under 'subtraction operation' in Exercise 8.3, Q5.)

mcqs.q: Which sum is correct?
mcqs.why: Only like terms combine: 5z + 3z = (5 + 3)z = 8z. Unlike terms like 2x and 3y cannot merge into 5xy, and a constant 7 cannot merge with 4y.

mcqs.q: 8x + 5x (Exercise 8.3, Q5 — listed as a subtraction-operation drill) equals:
mcqs.why: Add the coefficients: (8 + 5)x = 13x. Like terms with the same variable add directly.

lessons.title: Exercise 8.4 — Simplifying with Brackets; Finding Values
lessons.notes_html:
Removing brackets

Simplify from the innermost bracket outward, collecting like terms at each step. A minus sign before a bracket changes every sign inside it: 5a − (7a − 3b) = 5a − 7a + 3b.

Finding the value of an expression

Put the given number in place of the variable and calculate, watching the signs: if x = 2, then 3x = 6 and −5x = −10; if y = −3, then −3y = −3 × (−3) = +9.

Worked example (from Exercise 8.4, Q1)

Simplify: [x + x + (y + y + 2x)].

Step 1: Innermost bracket: y + y + 2x = 2y + 2x.

Step 2: Inside the square brackets: x + x + 2y + 2x = 4x + 2y.

Answer: 4x + 2y

mcqs.q: [5a − {3a + (3b − 6b + 4a)}] in simplest form is:
mcqs.why: Innermost: 3b − 6b + 4a = 4a − 3b. Braces: 3a + 4a − 3b = 7a − 3b. Then 5a − (7a − 3b) = 5a − 7a + 3b = −2a + 3b.

mcqs.q: When x = 2, the values of 3x and −5x are:
mcqs.why: Substitute x = 2: 3x = 3 × 2 = 6, and −5x = −5 × 2 = −10.

mcqs.q: When y = −3, the value of −3y is:
mcqs.why: −3y = −3 × (−3) = +9. A negative times a negative gives a positive.

mcqs.q: When a = 3, b = 5, c = 2, the value of a + b + c is:
mcqs.why: To find the value of an expression, replace each variable by its given value: a + b + c = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10.

mcqs.q: When a = 3, b = 5, c = 2, the value of 2a − 3b + c is:
A minus sign before a bracket:
options: Removes only the first sign inside
Changes every sign inside the bracket
mcqs.why: Subtracting a bracket changes the sign of every term inside it: −(7a − 3b) = −7a + 3b.

mcqs.q: When x = 5, the value of 4x − 3 is:
mcqs.why: Put x = 5 in the expression: 4x − 3 = 4 × 5 − 3 = 20 − 3 = 17. Remember 4x means 4 times x.

mcqs.q: [x + x + (y + y + 2x)] simplifies to:
mcqs.why: Innermost bracket: 2y + 2x. Then x + x + 2x = 4x, giving 4x + 2y.

mcqs.q: When p = −2, the value of p² is:
mcqs.why: p² = (−2) × (−2) = +4. Squaring a negative number gives a positive result.

mcqs.q: To find the value of an expression we:
options: Substitute the given value for the variable and calculate
mcqs.why: Evaluation means replacing each variable by its given value and then doing the arithmetic carefully, keeping the sign rules of integers.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 8 — Algebra Basics: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Words → symbols: "3 times x plus 5" = 3x + 5; "5 less than y" = y − 5; sum of 5a and 9b = 5a + 9b.
  • Terms are separated by + or −; variable = letter; constant = number-only term; coefficient = number with the variable.
  • Like terms (same variable part) can be added/subtracted by their coefficients.
  • Brackets: simplify innermost first; a − before a bracket flips all signs inside.
  • Value of an expression: substitute and calculate.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 8, Q1)

Write in symbols: "3 times x plus 5."

Step 1: 3 times x = 3x.

Step 2: Plus 5: 3x + 5.

Answer: 3x + 5

mcqs.q: 'The sum of 5a and 9b' in symbols is:
mcqs.why: Sum means addition, and the two unlike terms stay separate: 5a + 9b.

mcqs.q: '5 less than y' in symbols is:
mcqs.why: '5 less than y' means start from y and take 5 away: y − 5. (The book's printed wording for this item is garbled; the intended reading, as solved, is '5 less than y'.)

mcqs.q: '6 more than a number' (Review Q1(v) pattern) for the number t is:
mcqs.why: '6 more than a number' means the number increased by 6. For the number t this is written t + 6 — addition, in the same pattern as Review Exercise 8, Q1.

mcqs.q: The number of terms in 7x + 5 + 8 (Exercise 8.2) is:
mcqs.why: The expression has three terms: 7x, 5 and 8 — terms are counted by the + and − separators.

mcqs.q: 3x + 5x − 2x in simplest form is:
mcqs.why: Add and subtract coefficients of like terms: 3 + 5 − 2 = 6, giving 6x.

mcqs.q: When m = 4, the value of 7m − 5 is:
mcqs.why: Put m = 4 in the expression: 7m − 5 = 7 × 4 − 5 = 28 − 5 = 23. Multiply first, then subtract, following the order of operations.

mcqs.q: Which pair are like terms?
mcqs.why: 5pq and −2pq have exactly the same variable part pq, so they are like terms. The others differ in their variables (or one term is constant).

mcqs.q: 10y − 4y + y in simplest form is:
mcqs.why: 10 − 4 + 1 = 7 (plain y has coefficient 1), so the result is 7y.

mcqs.q: The coefficient of the variable in the term −x is:
mcqs.why: −x means −1 × x, so the numerical coefficient is −1.

mcqs.q: An expression with exactly two terms is built from:
options: Two parts separated by one + or − sign
mcqs.why: Terms are counted by +/− separators: one separator gives two terms, e.g. 2x + 3y or 4y + 7.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.1 — Forming One-Degree (Linear) Equations
lessons.notes_html:
From words to an equation

Call the unknown number x. Then translate the sentence:

  • "Sum of a number and 8 is 15" → x + 8 = 15
  • "Difference of a number and 20 is 2" → x − 20 = 2
  • "A number multiplied by 5 is 35" → 5x = 35
  • "Adding 4 to twice a number gives 20" → 2x + 4 = 20

An equation in which the variable has power 1 only is a one-degree (linear) equation.

Worked example (from Exercise 9.1, Q6)

Form an equation: "Subtracting fifteen from a number gives the answer 5."

Step 1: Suppose the required number is x.

Step 2: Subtracting fifteen from it is x − 15.

Step 3: This equals 5.

Answer: x − 15 = 5

mcqs.q: 'The difference of a number and 20 is two' as an equation (number = x) is:
mcqs.why: Difference of the number and 20 means x − 20, and 'is two' gives = 2. So the equation is x − 20 = 2.

mcqs.q: 'The sum of a number and 8 is 15' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: Sum means addition: x + 8, set equal to 15: x + 8 = 15.

mcqs.q: 'A number multiplied by 5 is 35' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: A number x multiplied by 5 is written 5x, so the equation is 5x = 35.

mcqs.q: 'Adding two to a number gives the answer 4' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: Adding two to the number x gives x + 2 = 4.

mcqs.q: 'Subtracting fifteen from a number gives 5' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: Subtracting 15 FROM the number means x − 15, equal to 5: x − 15 = 5.

mcqs.q: 'Adding 4 to twice a number gives 20' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: Twice the number is 2x; adding 4 gives 2x + 4 = 20.

mcqs.q: If my age is m and my father's age is f, 'my age is fifteen years more than my father's age' (Exercise 9.1, Q8) is:
mcqs.why: My age equals my father's age plus 15: m = f + 15.

mcqs.q: A one-degree (linear) equation is one in which:
options: The variable appears with power 1 only
mcqs.why: One-degree means the highest power of the variable is 1, as in x + 8 = 15 or 5x = 35.

mcqs.q: 'Sixteen divided by four equals 4' (Exercise 9.1, Q4) is:
options: An open statement with variable x
A numerical statement 16 ÷ 4 = 4 with no variable
mcqs.why: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 contains only numbers — the solved book itself notes this printed item has no variable. It is a true numerical statement, not an equation to solve.

mcqs.q: 'A number divided by 6 is 7' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: A number x divided by 6 is written x/6, set equal to 7: x/6 = 7.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.2 — Solving Linear Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The balance rule

An equation is like a balance: whatever you do to one side, do the same to the other side. Undo the operations around the variable one by one:

x + a = b → subtract a  •  x − a = b → add a  •  ax = b → divide by a  •  x/a = b → multiply by a

For two-step equations (like 6x + 1 = 49) first undo the + or −, then the × or ÷. Always check by putting the answer back into the equation.

Worked example (from Exercise 9.2, Q8)

Solve: 6x + 1 = 49.

Step 1: Subtract 1 from both sides: 6x = 48.

Step 2: Divide both sides by 6: x = 48 ÷ 6 = 8.

Step 3: Check: 6 × 8 + 1 = 49 ✓.

Answer: x = 8

mcqs.q: Solve x − 7 = 8:
mcqs.why: Add 7 to both sides: x = 8 + 7 = 15. Check: 15 − 7 = 8 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve y + 5 = 12:
mcqs.why: Subtract 5 from both sides: y = 12 − 5 = 7. Check: 7 + 5 = 12 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve 7y = 14:
mcqs.why: Divide both sides by 7: y = 14/7 = 2. Check: 7 × 2 = 14 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve 3x = 30:
mcqs.why: Undo the multiplication by dividing BOTH sides by 3: x = 30/3 = 10. Check: 3 × 10 = 30 ✓. Whatever is done to one side must be done to the other.

mcqs.q: Solve y − 16 = 2:
mcqs.why: Add 16 to both sides: y = 2 + 16 = 18. Check: 18 − 16 = 2 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve x/4 = 3:
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by 4: x = 3 × 4 = 12. Check: 12/4 = 3 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve 7y + 2 = 44:
mcqs.why: Subtract 2 from both sides: 7y = 42. Divide by 7: y = 6. Check: 7 × 6 + 2 = 44 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve 6 = x + 9:
mcqs.why: Subtract 9 from both sides: 6 − 9 = x, so x = −3. Check: −3 + 9 = 6 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve 9x − 21 = 78:
mcqs.why: Add 21 to both sides: 9x = 99. Divide by 9: x = 11. Check: 9 × 11 − 21 = 78 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve (6x − 4)/(2x + 2) = 2 (Exercise 9.2, Q13):
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by (2x + 2): 6x − 4 = 4x + 4. Subtract 4x: 2x − 4 = 4, so 2x = 8 and x = 4. Check: (24 − 4)/(8 + 2) = 20/10 = 2 ✓.

lessons.title: Exercise 9.3 — Word Problems with Linear Equations
lessons.notes_html:
The method

1. Read carefully and suppose the unknown is x. 2. Express the other quantity through x (e.g. "6 more" → x + 6). 3. Write the equation from the total or the given relation. 4. Solve it. 5. Check the answer in the story.

Worked example (from Exercise 9.3, Q2)

In a cricket match, Jamil and Salim together scored 84 runs. Jamil scored 12 runs more than Salim. Find Salim's score.

Step 1: Suppose Salim's score is x; then Jamil's score is x + 12.

Step 2: Equation: x + (x + 12) = 84, so 2x + 12 = 84.

Step 3: 2x = 72, so x = 36.

Answer: Salim scored 36 runs (and Jamil 48 runs).

mcqs.q: 44 pieces of glass are sewn in a red ghagra and a green choli; the ghagra has 6 more pieces than the choli. Pieces in the green choli:
mcqs.why: Let the choli have x pieces; the ghagra has x + 6. Equation: x + (x + 6) = 44 → 2x = 38 → x = 19 pieces (ghagra 25).

mcqs.q: The sum of a number and its double is 9. The number is:
mcqs.why: Let the number be x; its double is 2x. Equation: x + 2x = 9, so 3x = 9 and x = 3. Check: 3 + 6 = 9 ✓.

mcqs.q: Multiplying the sum of a number and 6 by 7 gives 77. The number is:
mcqs.why: Equation: 7(x + 6) = 77. Divide both sides by 7: x + 6 = 11, so x = 5.

mcqs.q: The sum of a quarter of a number and 6 is 42. The number is:
mcqs.why: Equation: x/4 + 6 = 42. Subtract 6: x/4 = 36. Multiply by 4: x = 144.

mcqs.q: A mother's and daughter's ages sum to 22 years; the daughter is 20 years younger than the mother. The daughter's age is:
mcqs.why: Let the daughter be x; the mother is x + 20. Equation: x + (x + 20) = 22 → 2x = 2 → x = 1 year (mother 21).

mcqs.q: Two facing pages of a book have page numbers summing to 155 (Exercise 9.3, Q7 pattern). The pages are:
mcqs.why: Facing pages are consecutive: x + (x + 1) = 155 → 2x = 154 → x = 77. The pages are 77 and 78.

mcqs.q: In word problems, the FIRST step is to:
options: Suppose the unknown quantity is x and express the others through x
mcqs.why: Every solved problem in this exercise begins: 'Suppose the required number is x' — then the other quantity is written with x (like x + 6 or x + 12) and the equation is formed.

mcqs.q: A number added to its triple gives 24. The number is:
mcqs.why: Equation: x + 3x = 24 → 4x = 24 → x = 6. This is the Exercise 9.3 method: make an equation from the words, then solve it step by step.

mcqs.q: After solving a word problem, we should:
options: Check the answer against the story's conditions
mcqs.why: Checking confirms the answer fits the story — e.g. for the ghagra problem, 19 + 25 = 44 ✓ and 25 is 6 more than 19 ✓.

mcqs.q: If one quantity is '12 more than' another quantity x, it is written:
mcqs.why: '12 more than x' means x plus 12: x + 12 — as used for Jamil's score in Exercise 9.3, Q2.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 9 — Linear Equations: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Expressions: sum of x and 4 = x + 4; 7 less than x = x − 7; x multiplied by 9 = 9x; y divided by 6 = y/6.
  • Form the equation from the sentence, then solve by doing the same operation to both sides.
  • Undo in reverse: first +/−, then ×/÷; for a fraction equation, multiply both sides by the denominator.
  • Always check by substituting back.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 9, Q3)

Solve: (y + 1)/2 = 5.

Step 1: Multiply both sides by 2: y + 1 = 10.

Step 2: Subtract 1 from both sides: y = 9.

Step 3: Check: (9 + 1)/2 = 5 ✓.

Answer: y = 9

mcqs.q: '7 less than a number x' as an expression is:
mcqs.why: '7 less than x' means x take away 7: x − 7.

mcqs.q: 'A number y divided by 6' as an expression is:
mcqs.why: Division of y by 6 is written as the fraction y/6.

mcqs.q: 'Subtracting 3 from a number x gives 10' as an equation is:
mcqs.why: Subtracting 3 from x gives x − 3, and it equals 10: x − 3 = 10.

mcqs.q: Solve 5x − 3 = 18:
mcqs.why: Add 3 to both sides: 5x = 21. Divide by 5: x = 21/5 = 4 1/5. Check: 5 × 21/5 − 3 = 18 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve (m − 1)/3 = 1:
mcqs.why: Multiply both sides by 3: m − 1 = 3. Add 1: m = 4. Check: (4 − 1)/3 = 1 ✓.

mcqs.q: Solve x + 2 = 8 (from Exercise 9.2):
mcqs.why: Subtract 2 from both sides: x = 8 − 2 = 6.

mcqs.q: Solve 8x = 32 (from Exercise 9.2):
mcqs.why: Divide both sides by the coefficient 8: x = 32/8 = 4. Check: 8 × 4 = 32 ✓.

mcqs.q: The product of a variable x and 8 (Review Q1(vi)) is written:
mcqs.why: Product means multiplication, written without a sign: 8x.

mcqs.q: To solve x/2 + 4 = x − 1/3, Exercise 9.2 first multiplies both sides by:
mcqs.why: Multiplying by 6 clears both fractions: 3x + 24 = 6x − 2, which then solves to x = 26/3 = 8 2/3.

mcqs.q: Checking a solution means:
options: Solving again by a different method only
Putting the value back into the original equation to see both sides equal
mcqs.why: A solution is checked by substitution: if both sides of the original equation become equal, the value is correct — every solved question in this unit ends with such a check.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.1 — Line Segments and Perpendiculars (Compass Constructions)
lessons.notes_html:
Line segment

A line segment has two fixed ends and a fixed length — e.g. the edge of a book or the side of a ruler. With a compass we can copy a segment onto a line, join segments end to end (their measures add), and find a difference segment (measures subtract).

Perpendicular from a point ON the line

With the point as centre, mark two points P and Q on the line at equal distances. Open the compass to more than half of PQ, draw arcs from P and Q above the line meeting at R. Join the point to R — that line is perpendicular (90°) to the given line.

Perpendicular from a point OUTSIDE the line

With the outside point as centre, draw an arc cutting the line at P and Q; then arcs from P and Q on the far side meeting at R; join the point to R.

Worked example (from Exercise 10.1, Q2)

Find the difference of segments LM = 2 cm and OP = 4 cm by geometry.

Step 1: Mark point A on a straight line; with the compass take the larger segment OP (4 cm) and draw an arc from A to get B.

Step 2: Open the compass to the smaller segment LM (2 cm) and from A draw an arc to get C (between A and B).

Step 3: The remaining part CB is the difference segment.

Answer: mCB = 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm.

mcqs.q: A line segment is:
options: A part of a line with two fixed ends and a fixed length
mcqs.why: A line segment has two endpoints and a definite length — like the edge of a book, a pencil, or the side of a door (Review Exercise 10, Q1).

mcqs.q: To find the difference segment of OP = 4 cm and LM = 2 cm by compass, the difference measures:
mcqs.why: The difference segment is what remains after marking the smaller segment inside the larger: 4 cm − 2 cm = 2 cm.

mcqs.q: If mAB = 4.3 cm, mCD = 3.5 cm and mEF = 2 cm, a segment equal to mAB + mCD + mEF (Review Q2) measures:
mcqs.why: Join the segments one after another on a straight line; their measures add: 4.3 + 3.5 + 2 = 9.8 cm.

mcqs.q: In the perpendicular construction from a point C on line AB, the first arc with centre C cuts AB at:
options: Two points P and Q at equal distances from C
mcqs.why: With C as centre and any suitable radius, the arc cuts AB on both sides of C, giving points P and Q equally distant from C.

mcqs.q: For the second step of the perpendicular construction, the compass is opened to:
mcqs.why: The two arcs from P and Q meet only if the compass opening is MORE than half of PQ. With exactly half or less, the arcs would not cross above the line.

mcqs.q: The line CR in the perpendicular construction makes an angle with AB of:
mcqs.why: A perpendicular line meets the given line at a right angle, 90°. That is the whole purpose of the construction.

mcqs.q: For a perpendicular from a point OUTSIDE the line, the first arc is drawn:
options: From any point on the line
With the outside point as centre, cutting the line at two points
mcqs.why: With the outside point C as centre and a wide enough opening, the arc cuts AB at two points P and Q; arcs from P and Q then meet at R on the far side, and CR is the perpendicular.

mcqs.q: Which instrument is used to copy the length of a segment in these constructions?
mcqs.why: The compass opening holds the length of a segment and transfers it onto a line — this is how segments are joined, copied and subtracted 'by geometry' in Exercise 10.1.

mcqs.q: Joining segments of 3 cm, 5 cm and 2 cm end to end gives a segment of:
mcqs.why: When segments are joined on a straight line, measures add: 3 + 5 + 2 = 10 cm.

mcqs.q: The difference of segments 7.5 cm and 3 cm, found by the compass method, is:
mcqs.why: Mark the 3 cm segment inside the 7.5 cm segment from the same starting point; the remaining part measures 7.5 − 3 = 4.5 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.2 — Bisecting Angles and Constructing Angles with a Compass
lessons.notes_html:
Bisecting an angle

To bisect an angle means to divide it into two equal parts. With the vertex as centre, draw an arc cutting both arms at P and Q. Open the compass to more than half of PQ; draw arcs from P and Q inside the angle meeting at R. The ray from the vertex through R is the bisector. An 80° angle bisects into two 40° angles.

Constructing standard angles

The basic compass angle is 60° (arc from a point on the ray with the same radius). Bisecting gives the family:

60° → 30° → 15°;   90° → 45° → 22½°

90° comes from a perpendicular construction; bisecting the angle between 60° and 90° gives 75°, and so on.

Worked example (from Exercise 10.2, Q4)

Construct an angle of 30°.

Step 1: Draw a ray OP. With O as centre, draw an arc cutting OP at A.

Step 2: With the same radius and A as centre, draw an arc cutting the first arc at B — angle AOB is 60°.

Step 3: Bisect angle AOB with arcs from A and B; join O to their crossing point R.

Answer: m∠POR = 30°.

mcqs.q: Bisecting an angle of 80° gives two angles of:
mcqs.why: Bisect means divide into two EQUAL parts: 80° ÷ 2 = 40° each.

mcqs.q: In the bisection construction, the first arc is drawn with centre at:
mcqs.why: The arc is drawn with the VERTEX as centre, so that it cuts both arms at points P and Q equally distant from the vertex.

mcqs.q: The ray BR in the bisection of angle ABC is called:
mcqs.why: The ray from the vertex through the crossing point of the two arcs divides the angle into two equal parts — it is the angle's bisector.

mcqs.q: Bisecting a 90° angle gives:
mcqs.why: 90° ÷ 2 = 45°. Bisecting once more gives 22½° — one of the angles constructed in Exercise 10.2, Q4.

mcqs.q: The first standard angle obtained with a compass on a ray (arc from A with the same radius) is:
mcqs.why: With the same radius, the arc from A cuts the first arc at B such that triangle OAB is equilateral — the angle at O is 60°. Bisecting it gives 30°.

mcqs.q: To construct 22½°, we:
mcqs.why: 22½° is half of 45°, and 45° is itself half of 90°. So: construct 90°, bisect to 45°, bisect again to 22½°.

mcqs.q: Bisecting an angle of 70° gives two angles of:
mcqs.why: To bisect means to divide into two equal parts: 70° ÷ 2 = 35°. So each of the two angles formed by the bisector measures 35°.

mcqs.q: When copying a given angle (Exercise 10.2, Q3), the given angle's measure is first found with:
mcqs.why: The book's method: measure the printed angle with a protractor (in the figure about 45°), then construct an equal angle with the compass and bisect it as asked.

mcqs.q: The arcs from P and Q in bisection must be drawn with:
options: An opening equal to PQ exactly
The same opening, more than half of PQ
mcqs.why: Both arcs use the SAME compass opening, greater than half of PQ, so that they cross at a point R which lies on the bisector.

mcqs.q: An angle of 75° can be constructed as:
options: The bisector of the angle between 60° and 90°
mcqs.why: 75° is midway between the compass angles 60° and 90°: (60 + 90)/2 = 75, obtained by bisecting the angle between the 60° and 90° rays.

lessons.title: Exercise 10.3 — Constructing Triangles
lessons.notes_html:
Four construction cases

  • SSS — three sides given: draw the longest side; arcs from its ends with the other two lengths meet at the third vertex.
  • SAS — two sides and the INCLUDED angle: draw one side, make the angle at its end, mark the second side on the new arm, join.
  • ASA — one side and two angles: draw the side, construct the two angles at its ends; the arms meet at the third vertex.
  • RHS — right triangle with hypotenuse and one side: draw a side, erect a 90° angle, and cut it with an arc of the hypotenuse length.

Worked example (from Exercise 10.3, Q1)

Construct triangle ABC with mAB = 3 cm, mBC = 5 cm, mCA = 7 cm (SSS).

Step 1: Draw the longest side AC = 7 cm with a scale.

Step 2: Open the compass to AB = 3 cm; with A as centre draw an arc.

Step 3: Open the compass to BC = 5 cm; with C as centre draw an arc cutting the first arc at B.

Step 4: Join B to A and C.

Answer: △ABC is the required triangle.

mcqs.q: Constructing a triangle with sides 3 cm, 5 cm, 7 cm is the case called:
mcqs.why: All three sides are given and no angle — this is the SSS (three-sides) construction of Exercise 10.3, Q1.

mcqs.q: In the SSS construction, we draw first:
mcqs.why: The method draws the longest side first (AC = 7 cm), then strikes arcs of the other two lengths from its endpoints.

mcqs.q: Triangle MNO with m∠N = 63°, mNO = 3 cm, mMN = 5 cm is the case:
options: SAS — two sides and the included angle
mcqs.why: The angle N lies BETWEEN the two given sides NO and MN, so it is the SAS case (Exercise 10.3, Q5). Note 63° is not a standard compass angle, so a protractor is used for it in practice.

mcqs.q: Triangle PQR with mPQ = 5 cm, m∠Q = 40°, m∠P = 60° is the case:
options: ASA — one side and two angles
mcqs.why: One side and the two angles at its ends are given — the ASA construction (Exercise 10.3, Q9). The third angle is 180° − 60° − 40° = 80°.

mcqs.q: Right triangle XYZ with m∠Z = 90°, hypotenuse mXY = 7 cm and mXZ = 5 cm is the case:
options: RHS — hypotenuse and one side of a right triangle
mcqs.why: A right angle, the hypotenuse and one side are given — the RHS construction (Exercise 10.3, Q13).

mcqs.q: In an SAS construction, the given angle must be:
options: The angle included between the two given sides
mcqs.why: SAS works because the angle is INCLUDED between the two sides: draw a side, make the angle at its endpoint, and mark the second side along the angle's other arm.

mcqs.q: For triangle ABC with sides 2 cm, 5 cm, 5 cm (Exercise 10.3, Q2), the construction is:
options: SSS, with arcs of 2 cm and 5 cm from the ends of the 5 cm base
mcqs.why: It is again SSS: draw one 5 cm side, then arcs of 2 cm and 5 cm from its ends meet at the third vertex. The triangle is isosceles.

mcqs.q: A triangle CANNOT be constructed with sides:
mcqs.why: The two shorter sides must together exceed the longest side: 2 + 3 = 5 < 9, so the arcs would never meet — no triangle exists with sides 2, 3, 9.

mcqs.q: In the ASA construction, the two constructed angles are made:
options: At the midpoint of the side
At the two ends of the given side
mcqs.why: The angles are constructed at the two ENDPOINTS of the given side; their arms meet at the third vertex of the triangle.

mcqs.q: The instrument pair used for all these constructions is:
mcqs.why: Lengths are transferred with the compass and straight edges are drawn with the ruler/scale — the standard construction pair used throughout Unit 10 (a protractor is used only for non-standard given angles like 63°).

lessons.title: Review Exercise 10 — Geometry: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Line segments can be copied, joined (measures add) and subtracted (measures subtract) with a compass.
  • Perpendicular from a point on/off a line: equal marks P, Q, then arcs opened to more than half of PQ.
  • Angle bisector divides an angle into two equal parts; standard compass angles: 60°, 90°, and their halves 30°, 45°, 22½°.
  • Triangles are constructed in four cases: SSS, SAS, ASA, RHS.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 10, Q2)

Find a segment equal to mAB + mCD + mEF where mAB = 4.3 cm, mCD = 3.5 cm, mEF = 2 cm.

Step 1: On a straight line, take the three measures one after another with the compass.

Step 2: Add: 4.3 + 3.5 + 2 = 9.8.

Answer: The required line segment measures 9.8 cm.

mcqs.q: Which of these is an example of a line segment from daily life?
mcqs.why: The edge of a book has two fixed ends and a fixed length — Review Exercise 10, Q1 lists it first among examples (also a pencil, the side of a door, the side of a scale).

mcqs.q: A segment equal to mAB − mCD, where mAB = 4.3 cm and mCD = 3.5 cm (Review Q2 pattern), measures:
mcqs.why: Difference of measures: 4.3 − 3.5 = 0.8 cm — found by marking the smaller segment inside the larger with a compass.

mcqs.q: The bisector of a 50° angle makes angles of:
mcqs.why: A bisector halves the angle: 50° ÷ 2 = 25°.

mcqs.q: To construct a perpendicular at a point on a line, after marking P and Q the arcs must cross:
mcqs.why: The arcs from P and Q, opened to more than half of PQ, cross at a point R off the line; joining R to the given point gives the perpendicular.

mcqs.q: Which data set is an SAS case?
options: Side 6 cm with angles 40° and 70° at its ends
Hypotenuse 10 cm and side 6 cm in a right triangle
Sides 4 cm and 6 cm with the 50° angle between them
mcqs.why: SAS = two sides with the INCLUDED angle between them. The others are SSS, ASA and RHS respectively.

mcqs.q: Constructing 15° is done by:
mcqs.why: Each bisection halves the angle: 60° → 30° → 15°. So two bisections of the standard 60° angle give 15°.

mcqs.q: In △ABC construction with mAB = 8 cm, mBC = 6 cm, mCA = 10 cm (Exercise 10.3, Q4), the side drawn first is:
mcqs.why: The SSS method starts with the longest side, CA = 10 cm, then arcs of 8 cm and 6 cm from C and A meet at B.

mcqs.q: The sum of the angles in any triangle is:
mcqs.why: The three angles of a triangle always total 180° — used in ASA problems, e.g. 60° + 40° leaves 80° for the third angle.

mcqs.q: A perpendicular line is one that meets another line at:
mcqs.why: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle, 90° — the constructions of Exercise 10.1 produce exactly this.

mcqs.q: In Review Exercise 10, the four daily-life examples of a line segment include:
options: Edge of a book, a pencil, side of a door/wall, side of a scale
mcqs.why: The solved answer lists: (1) the edge of a book, (2) a pencil or pen, (3) the side of a room wall or door, (4) the side of a scale — each has two fixed ends and a fixed length.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.1 — Perimeter and Area of Squares and Rectangles
lessons.notes_html:
Square

Perimeter of a square = 4 × side  •  Area of a square = side × side

Rectangle

Perimeter of a rectangle = 2 × (length + breadth)  •  Area of a rectangle = length × breadth

Perimeter is measured in cm or m; area in cm² or m². For a figure with a piece cut out, area = area of the whole − area of the cut-out, while the perimeter is found by adding all the boundary sides. Backwards: side of a square = perimeter ÷ 4.

Worked example (from Exercise 11.1, Q2)

Find the perimeter and area of rectangle ZYXW with length 6 cm and breadth 2.5 cm.

Step 1: Perimeter = 2(6 + 2.5) = 2 × 8.5 = 17 cm.

Step 2: Area = 6 × 2.5 = 15 cm².

Answer: Perimeter 17 cm, area 15 cm².

mcqs.q: Square EFGH has each side 3.5 cm. Its perimeter and area are:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 × 3.5 = 14 cm. Area = 3.5 × 3.5 = 12.25 cm².

mcqs.q: A square of side 5 cm (Exercise 11.1 pattern) has area:
mcqs.why: Area of a square = side × side = 5 × 5 = 25 cm². (Its perimeter would be 20 cm — do not mix the two.)

mcqs.q: Rectangle OTSR has length 5 cm and breadth 3 cm. Its perimeter is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 2(length + breadth) = 2(5 + 3) = 16 cm. Its area is 5 × 3 = 15 cm².

mcqs.q: Rectangle ONML has length 10 cm and breadth 2 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area = length × breadth = 10 × 2 = 20 cm². (Perimeter = 2(10 + 2) = 24 cm.)

mcqs.q: A rectangle of length 4.8 cm and breadth 2.7 cm has area:
mcqs.why: Area of a rectangle = length × breadth = 4.8 × 2.7 = 12.96 cm². Area is always written in square units.

mcqs.q: The side of a square whose perimeter is 48 cm (Exercise 11.1, Q3 pattern) is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 × side, so side = 48 ÷ 4 = 12 cm.

mcqs.q: A 6 cm × 6 cm square has a 2 cm × 3 cm rectangle cut out (figure POIN). The remaining area is:
mcqs.why: Area left = area of big square − area of cut-out = (6 × 6) − (2 × 3) = 36 − 6 = 30 cm². (The perimeter of this figure is 30 cm by adding all boundary sides.)

mcqs.q: Perimeter is measured in ______ and area in ______.
mcqs.why: Perimeter is a length (cm, m). Area measures surface, so it uses square units (cm², m²).

mcqs.q: A rectangle of length 5 cm and breadth 2.5 cm (Exercise 11.1, Q3 pattern) has perimeter:
If the area of a square is 36 cm², its side is:
mcqs.why: Area = side × side = 36, and 6 × 6 = 36, so the side is 6 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.2 — Area of a Path (Shaded Part)
lessons.notes_html:
The path rule

For a path around or inside a rectangle:

Area of path = area of outer rectangle − area of inner rectangle

If the path of width w is INSIDE, the inner length and breadth each shrink by 2w (the path comes on both sides). If the path is OUTSIDE, the outer length and breadth each grow by 2w.

Worked example (from Exercise 11.2, Q1(ii))

Outer rectangle 35 cm × 25 cm with a path 10 cm wide inside. Find the area of the path.

Step 1: Inner length = 35 − 10 − 10 = 15 cm; inner breadth = 25 − 10 − 10 = 5 cm.

Step 2: Area of path = (35 × 25) − (15 × 5) = 875 − 75.

Answer: 800 cm².

mcqs.q: Outer rectangle 25 cm × 20 cm, path 5 cm wide inside. The inner rectangle measures:
mcqs.why: The path takes 5 cm from BOTH ends of each side: length 25 − 5 − 5 = 15 cm, breadth 20 − 5 − 5 = 10 cm.

mcqs.q: For the same figure (25 × 20, path 5 cm inside), the area of the path is:
mcqs.why: Path area = outer area − inner area = (25 × 20) − (15 × 10) = 500 − 150 = 350 cm².

mcqs.q: Outer rectangle 50.5 cm × 40.5 cm and inner rectangle 45.5 cm × 35.5 cm. The shaded (path) area is:
A field 35 m × 30 m has a 5 m wide path inside it. The area of the path is:
A field 20 m × 10 m has a 5 m wide path OUTSIDE it. The outer measurement becomes:
mcqs.why: An outside path ADDS its width on both sides: length 20 + 5 + 5 = 30 m, breadth 10 + 5 + 5 = 20 m.

mcqs.q: For that outside-path figure, the area of the path is:
mcqs.why: Path area = outer area − field area = (30 × 20) − (20 × 10) = 600 − 200 = 400 m².

mcqs.q: A path of width w inside a rectangle reduces the inner length by:
mcqs.why: The path runs along both ends of the length, so the inner length = outer length − 2w. The same holds for the breadth.

mcqs.q: The general formula for the area of a path is:
options: Outer perimeter × width only in all cases
mcqs.why: Shaded path area = area of the outer rectangle − area of the inner (unshaded) rectangle — the method of every question in Exercise 11.2.

mcqs.q: Outer rectangle 40 m × 25 m, inner 36 m × 21 m (Review pattern). Path area:
If a path is 2 m wide, the difference between outer and inner length is:
mcqs.why: Check with the Review figure: outer 40 m, inner 36 m — difference 4 m = 2 × path width (2 m on each side).

lessons.title: Exercise 11.3 — Perimeter and Area in Daily Life (Costs and Missing Sides)
lessons.notes_html:
Fencing and grass costs

Fencing goes around the boundary, so first find the perimeter, then:

Cost of fencing = perimeter × rate per metre

Covering a floor or field uses the area: cost = area × rate per m². A missing side comes from area: length = area ÷ breadth.

Worked example (from Exercise 11.3, Q1)

Find the cost of fencing a square field of side 250 m at Rs 30 per metre.

Step 1: Perimeter = 4 × 250 = 1,000 m.

Step 2: Cost = 1,000 × 30 = Rs 30,000.

Answer: Rs 30,000.

mcqs.q: Fencing a rectangular field 250 m long and 150 m wide at Rs 30 per metre costs:
Basma's field is 210 m × 100 m and Amima's is 150 m × 100 m (Exercise 11.3, Q3). Whose fencing distance is greater?
mcqs.why: Basma's perimeter = 2(210 + 100) = 620 m; Amima's = 2(150 + 100) = 500 m. Basma's is greater.

mcqs.q: A piece of land has breadth 15 m and area 615 m². Its length is:

A path 120 m long and 8 m wide is paved at Rs 200 per m² (Exercise 11.3, Q6). The cost is:
A floor is covered with 650 bricks, each of area 0.5 m². The area of the floor is:

mcqs.q: For fencing cost we multiply the rate by the:
mcqs.why: A fence runs around the boundary of the field, so its length is the perimeter. Cost = perimeter × rate per metre.

mcqs.q: For the cost of laying grass or tiles we multiply the rate by the:
mcqs.why: Grass and tiles COVER the surface, so the quantity needed depends on the area: cost = area × rate per square metre.

mcqs.q: A rectangular field has area 480 m² and length 24 m. Its breadth is:
mcqs.why: Breadth = area ÷ length = 480 ÷ 24 = 20 m.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.4 — Area of a Parallelogram; Altitude
lessons.notes_html:
Altitude

The altitude of a parallelogram (or triangle, or trapezium) is the perpendicular distance from a vertex to the opposite side (the base). In parallelogram LMON, OP perpendicular to LM is the altitude, OP = 4.5 cm, with base LM.

Area of a parallelogram

Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude

Use the altitude belonging to that base — the perpendicular height, not the slanted side. Backwards: base = area ÷ altitude; altitude = area ÷ base.

Worked example (from Exercise 11.4, Q2)

Find the area of a parallelogram with base 15 cm and altitude 8 cm.

Step 1: Area = base × altitude.

Step 2: Area = 15 × 8 = 120.

Answer: 120 cm².

mcqs.q: The altitude of a figure is:
options: The perpendicular distance from a vertex to the opposite side (base)
mcqs.why: An altitude is always a PERPENDICULAR segment from a vertex to the base — e.g. in parallelogram LMON, OP ⊥ LM is the altitude to base LM.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has base 10 cm and altitude 6 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area = base × altitude = 10 × 6 = 60 cm².

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has base 4.5 cm and altitude 5.5 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of a parallelogram = base × altitude = 4.5 × 5.5 = 24.75 cm². The altitude is the perpendicular height belonging to the base.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has area 192 cm² and altitude 12 cm. Its base is:
mcqs.why: Base = area ÷ altitude = 192 ÷ 12 = 16 cm.

mcqs.q: The base of a parallelogram is 15 m and its area is 180 m² (Exercise 11.4, Q4 pattern). Its altitude is:
mcqs.why: Altitude = area ÷ base = 180 ÷ 15 = 12 m.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has area 4.50 m² and altitude 1.5 m. Its base is:
mcqs.why: Base = area ÷ altitude = 4.50 ÷ 1.5 = 3 m.

mcqs.q: In trapezium PQRS, SZ is perpendicular to PR with SZ = 4 cm (Exercise 11.4, Q1). SZ is:
mcqs.why: SZ is drawn perpendicular from vertex S to the side PR, so SZ = 4 cm is the altitude belonging to base PR.

mcqs.q: In triangle XYT, YT is perpendicular to XT and YT = 6 cm. The altitude is:
mcqs.why: The perpendicular from vertex Y to base XT is YT, so the altitude is 6 cm with base XT.

mcqs.q: The area of a parallelogram with base 7 cm and altitude 9 cm is:
mcqs.why: Area = base × altitude = 7 × 9 = 63 cm². For a parallelogram, always multiply the base by its own altitude (the perpendicular height), not by the slant side.

mcqs.q: To find the area of a parallelogram we need:
options: One base and its altitude (perpendicular height)
mcqs.why: Area = base × altitude. Only the chosen base and the perpendicular distance to the opposite side are needed — the slanted side is not used.

lessons.title: Exercise 11.5 — Area of a Trapezium and a Triangle
lessons.notes_html:
Trapezium

A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides. Its area is:

Area of a trapezium = ½ × altitude × (sum of the parallel sides)

Triangle

Area of a triangle = ½ × base × altitude

A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two equal triangles, so a triangle's area is half the parallelogram's on the same base and altitude.

Worked example (from Exercise 11.5, Q2)

The parallel sides of a trapezium are 6 cm and 8 cm and its altitude is 5 cm. Find its area.

Step 1: Area = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides) = ½ × 5 × (6 + 8).

Step 2: = ½ × 5 × 14 = 35.

Answer: 35 cm².

mcqs.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 5 cm and 6 cm and altitude 4 cm. Its area is:
A trapezium has parallel sides 3.5 cm and 4.5 cm and altitude 2 cm. Its area is:
A trapezium has parallel sides 15 cm and 20 cm and area 140 cm². Its altitude is:
mcqs.why: 140 = ½ × altitude × 35, so altitude = (140 × 2) ÷ 35 = 8 cm.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 8 cm and altitude 6 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of triangle = ½ × base × altitude = ½ × 8 × 6 = 24 cm².

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 7 cm and altitude 2.5 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × altitude = ½ × 7 × 2.5 = 8.75 cm². The ½ comes because a triangle is half of the parallelogram on the same base and altitude.

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 6.5 cm and altitude 3.5 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × altitude = ½ × 6.5 × 3.5 = 11.375 cm².

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 6 cm and altitude 5 cm (Exercise 11.5, Q5 pattern). Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × altitude = ½ × 6 × 5 = 15 cm² (Exercise 11.5, Q5 pattern).

mcqs.q: A triangle's area is 40 m² and its base is 5 m (Exercise 11.5, Q6 pattern). Its altitude is:
mcqs.why: 40 = ½ × 5 × altitude, so altitude = (40 × 2) ÷ 5 = 16 m.

mcqs.q: In the figure of Exercise 11.5, Q7, a parallelogram is divided by a diagonal and one triangle (area 20 cm²) is shaded. The area of the parallelogram is:
mcqs.why: A diagonal divides a parallelogram into two EQUAL triangles, so the parallelogram's area = 2 × 20 = 40 cm².

mcqs.q: The formula for the area of a trapezium uses:
options: Half the altitude times the sum of the parallel sides
The sum of all four sides
The product of the parallel sides
mcqs.why: Area of trapezium = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides). The non-parallel sides are not used.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 11 — Perimeter & Area: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Square: P = 4 × side, A = side². Rectangle: P = 2(l + b), A = l × b.
  • Path area = outer area − inner area (inner sides shrink by 2 × width; outer sides grow by 2 × width).
  • Fencing cost = perimeter × rate; covering cost = area × rate.
  • Parallelogram: A = base × altitude. Triangle: A = ½ × base × altitude. Trapezium: A = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides).

Worked example (from Review Exercise 11)

Find the area of a trapezium with parallel sides 3 cm and 10 cm and altitude 2.5 cm.

Step 1: Area = ½ × altitude × (sum of parallel sides) = ½ × 2.5 × (3 + 10).

Step 2: = ½ × 2.5 × 13 = 16.25.

Answer: 16.25 cm².

mcqs.q: A square has each side 5.3 cm. Its perimeter and area are:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 × 5.3 = 21.2 cm. Area = 5.3 × 5.3 = 28.09 cm².

mcqs.q: A rectangle has length 11 cm and breadth 8 cm. Its perimeter and area are:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 2(11 + 8) = 38 cm. Area = 11 × 8 = 88 cm².

mcqs.q: A triangle has base 6 cm and altitude 2.5 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × altitude = ½ × 6 × 2.5 = 7.5 cm² — half of 15 cm², the area of the matching parallelogram.

mcqs.q: A parallelogram has base 8 cm and altitude 6 cm. Its area is:
mcqs.why: Area = base × altitude = 8 × 6 = 48 cm². For a parallelogram, always multiply the base by its own altitude (the perpendicular height), not by the slant side.

mcqs.q: A trapezium has parallel sides 3 cm and 10 cm and altitude 2.5 cm. Its area is:
The shaded path area for outer 40 m × 25 m and inner 36 m × 21 m is:
Which formula gives the area of a triangle?
mcqs.why: A triangle is half of the parallelogram on the same base and altitude, so its area = ½ × base × altitude.

mcqs.q: A square field of side 40 m is fenced at Rs 20 per metre. The cost is:
mcqs.why: Perimeter = 4 × 40 = 160 m. Cost = 160 × 20 = Rs 3,200.

mcqs.q: The altitude of a parallelogram must be drawn:
mcqs.why: Altitude is by definition the perpendicular distance from a vertex to the line of the base — a slanted side is never the altitude (unless the figure is a rectangle).

mcqs.q: A rectangle's length is 12 cm and area 96 cm². Its breadth and perimeter are:
mcqs.why: Breadth = 96 ÷ 12 = 8 cm. Perimeter = 2(12 + 8) = 40 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.1 — 3-D Shapes Around Us; Faces, Edges and Vertices
lessons.notes_html:
Shapes in daily life

  • Football → sphere
  • Ghee tin, glass of water → cylinder
  • Birthday cap → cone
  • Die → cube
  • Matchbox, milk carton → cuboid

Parts of a solid

A face is a flat surface, an edge is where two faces meet, and a vertex is a corner point. A cuboid and a cube both have:

6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices

A cone has 1 circular face (its base) and a pointed vertex (apex). Surface area is measured in square units (cm², m²); volume in cubic units (cm³, m³).

Worked example (from Exercise 12.1, Q2)

Fill in the blanks for a cuboid: number of edges, faces, vertices.

Step 1: Count the faces: top, bottom and four sides = 6.

Step 2: Count the edges: 4 on top, 4 on bottom, 4 vertical = 12.

Step 3: Count the corner points (vertices) = 8.

Answer: Edges 12, faces 6, vertices 8.

mcqs.q: The shape of a football is a:
mcqs.why: A football is round in every direction with no flat face — it is a sphere.

mcqs.q: The shape of a ghee tin is a:
mcqs.why: A ghee tin has two circular ends joined by a curved surface — a cylinder (like a glass of water or a tin, Review Exercise 12).

mcqs.q: The shape of a birthday cap is a:
mcqs.why: A birthday cap has a circular base and rises to a point — a cone.

mcqs.q: The shape of a die is a:
mcqs.why: A die has all its edges equal and 6 square faces — a cube.

mcqs.q: A matchbox and a milk carton are examples of a:
mcqs.why: Their length, breadth and height are different, with 6 rectangular faces — a cuboid.

mcqs.q: A cuboid has:
mcqs.why: Cuboid (and cube): 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices — the blanks of Exercise 12.1, Q2(i).

mcqs.q: In the cube figure of Exercise 12.1, Q2(iii), AB shows ______ and point A shows ______:
mcqs.why: AB is a line where two faces meet — an edge. Point A is a corner — a vertex. The cube has 6 faces.

mcqs.q: A cone has how many circular faces?
mcqs.why: A cone has exactly one circular face, its flat base; the rest is a curved surface rising to the apex (vertex).

mcqs.q: The volume of a cuboid is measured in ______ and its surface area in ______ (Practical Work, Unit 12):
mcqs.why: Volume fills space, so it is measured in cubic units (cm³, m³). Surface area covers a surface, so it is measured in square units (cm², m²).

mcqs.q: Point A at the top of the cone figure (Exercise 12.1, Q2(ii)) shows:
mcqs.why: The pointed top of a cone is its vertex, also called the apex.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.2 — Surface Area and Volume of a Cuboid and a Cube
lessons.notes_html:
Cuboid (length l, breadth b, height h)

Surface area = 2(lb + bh + hl)  •  Volume = l × b × h

Cube (side s)

Surface area = 6 × s²  •  Volume = s × s × s

Surface area counts all six faces; volume counts the space inside.

Worked example (from Exercise 12.2, Q1)

Find the surface area and volume of a cuboid with length 6 cm, breadth 5 cm, height 8 cm.

Step 1: Surface area = 2(6×5 + 5×8 + 8×6) = 2(30 + 40 + 48) = 2 × 118 = 236 cm².

Step 2: Volume = 6 × 5 × 8 = 240 cm³.

Answer: Surface area 236 cm², volume 240 cm³.

mcqs.q: A cuboid of 3 mm × 4 mm × 5 mm has surface area and volume:
A cube of side 2 cm has surface area and volume:
mcqs.why: Surface area = 6 × (2 × 2) = 24 cm². Volume = 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 cm³.

mcqs.q: A cuboid of 6.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 3 cm has volume:
mcqs.why: Volume = 6.5 × 2.5 × 3 = 48.75 cm³. (Its surface area is 2(16.25 + 7.5 + 19.5) = 86.5 cm².)

mcqs.q: A cube of side 3.5 cm has surface area:
mcqs.why: Surface area = 6 × (3.5 × 3.5) = 6 × 12.25 = 73.5 cm². (Its volume is 42.875 cm³.)

mcqs.q: The surface area formula of a cuboid is:
mcqs.why: A cuboid has three pairs of equal faces: lb, bh and hl — each counted twice: 2(lb + bh + hl).

mcqs.q: The volume of a cube of side 4 cm is:
mcqs.why: Volume = side × side × side = 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 cm³.

mcqs.q: A cuboid has length 10 cm, breadth 4 cm, height 3 cm. Its volume is:
mcqs.why: Volume = l × b × h = 10 × 4 × 3 = 120 cm³.

mcqs.q: Surface area is measured in ______ units and volume in ______ units:
mcqs.why: Surface area covers faces → square units (cm²). Volume fills space → cubic units (cm³). This matches the Practical Work blanks of Unit 12.

mcqs.q: A cube of side 5 cm has surface area:
mcqs.why: Surface area = 6 × (5 × 5) = 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

mcqs.q: A cuboid's volume is 60 cm³ with length 5 cm and breadth 3 cm. Its height is:
mcqs.why: Volume = l × b × h → 60 = 5 × 3 × h = 15h, so h = 60 ÷ 15 = 4 cm.

lessons.title: Exercise 12.3 — Surface Area and Volume in Daily Life
lessons.notes_html:
Polishing and painting use surface area

Cost = surface area × rate per m². Capacity of a tank means its volume.

Worked example (from Exercise 12.3, Q1)

Find the cost of polishing a cupboard at Rs 500 per m², if its sides are 3 m, 2 m and 1 m.

Step 1: Surface area = 2(3×2 + 2×1 + 1×3) = 2(6 + 2 + 3) = 22 m².

Step 2: Cost = 22 × 500 = Rs 11,000.

Answer: Rs 11,000.

mcqs.q: A tank is 5 m long, 4 m wide and 2.5 m high. Its capacity is:
mcqs.why: Capacity = volume = 5 × 4 × 2.5 = 50 m³. The capacity of a box-shaped tank is its volume: length × width × height, worked out step by step.

mcqs.q: A brick measures 25 cm × 10 cm × 4.5 cm. The space occupied by 1000 such bricks is:
mcqs.why: One brick: 25 × 10 × 4.5 = 1125 cm³. For 1000 bricks: 1,125,000 cm³ = 1.125 m³.

mcqs.q: Painting a cube-shaped tin box of side 2.5 m at Rs 50 per m² costs:
The capacity of a cube-shaped oil tank of side 5 m is:
mcqs.why: Capacity = volume of cube = 5 × 5 × 5 = 125 m³.

mcqs.q: Polishing or painting cost is calculated from the:
mcqs.why: Polish and paint cover the SURFACE of the solid, so we use surface area × rate per square metre — as in the cupboard question.

mcqs.q: The cost of tin for a cuboid of sides 5 m, 6 m, 7 m at Rs 100 per m² (Review pattern) is:
A water tank 3 m × 2 m × 1.5 m can hold:
mcqs.why: Capacity means volume: 3 × 2 × 1.5 = 9 m³. The tank can hold 9 cubic metres of water.

mcqs.q: How many litres are in 1 m³? (1 m³ = 1000 litres — capacity conversion used with tanks)
mcqs.why: One cubic metre holds 1000 litres, so the 50 m³ tank of Exercise 12.3, Q2 holds 50,000 litres.

mcqs.q: A cuboid box has volume 240 cm³ (from Exercise 12.2: 6 × 5 × 8). If it is filled with 1 cm cubes, the number of cubes is:
mcqs.why: Each 1 cm cube occupies 1 cm³, so a volume of 240 cm³ needs exactly 240 unit cubes.

mcqs.q: To find how much space 1000 bricks occupy, we use:
mcqs.why: Space occupied is volume: volume of one brick (1125 cm³) × 1000 = 1,125,000 cm³.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 12 — 3-D Shapes: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Daily-life shapes: football = sphere, tin/glass = cylinder, birthday cap = cone, die = cube, matchbox = cuboid.
  • Cube and cuboid: 6 faces, 12 edges, 8 vertices.
  • Cuboid: SA = 2(lb + bh + hl), V = lbh. Cube: SA = 6s², V = s³.
  • Painting/polishing → surface area; capacity/space → volume.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 12, Q3)

Find the surface area and volume of a cube of side 2.5 cm.

Step 1: Surface area = 6 × (2.5 × 2.5) = 6 × 6.25 = 37.5 cm².

Step 2: Volume = 2.5 × 2.5 × 2.5 = 15.625 cm³.

Answer: Surface area 37.5 cm², volume 15.625 cm³.

mcqs.q: A cuboid of 3.5 cm × 2 cm × 1.5 cm has surface area and volume:
The volume of a cube of side 2.5 cm (Review Q4) is:
mcqs.why: Volume of a cube = side × side × side = 2.5 × 2.5 × 2.5 = 15.625 cm³ (Review Exercise 12, Q4).

mcqs.q: Three daily-life examples of 3-D shapes (Review Q2) are:
mcqs.why: The Review answer gives: football — sphere; matchbox — cuboid; a glass of water or a tin — cylinder.

mcqs.q: A cube has how many faces, edges and vertices?
mcqs.why: Like the cuboid, a cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

mcqs.q: The volume of a cuboid 8 cm × 5 cm × 2 cm is:
mcqs.why: Volume of a cuboid = length × breadth × height = 8 × 5 × 2 = 80 cm³. Volume is always written in cubic units.

mcqs.q: A cuboid's surface area is 236 cm² (6 × 5 × 8 cuboid). Doubling only its height would:
mcqs.why: Volume = l × b × h is directly proportional to h: doubling h doubles the volume (240 → 480 cm³), while the surface area grows by less than double.

mcqs.q: Which solid has NO vertex?
mcqs.why: A sphere is perfectly round with no corner point at all — no vertex, no edge, no flat face.

mcqs.q: The surface area of a cube of side 10 cm is:
mcqs.why: Surface area = 6 × (10 × 10) = 6 × 100 = 600 cm².

mcqs.q: Capacity of a container means its:
mcqs.why: Capacity is the amount a container can hold — its volume, as with the tanks in Exercise 12.3.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.1 — Data, Tally Marks, Grouped and Ungrouped Data
lessons.notes_html:
Data

Data is a set of information and facts. The numerical facts we get in daily life are called data — for example, the marks of students or the number of visitors each week.

Ungrouped and grouped data

Ungrouped data is shown individually, in its original (raw) form — like a list of each student's marks. Grouped data is arranged into groups or intervals — like "price 512–611 → 8 books".

Tally marks

When collecting data (Practical Work: students' birth months), make one tally mark for each item; draw the fifth mark diagonally across the previous four, making bundles of five that are easy to count.

Worked example (from Exercise 13.1, Q3)

Which table shows grouped data: (i) each student's exam marks listed by name; (ii) Raza's book-store table: price interval 512–611 → 8 books, 612–711 → 5 books, ...?

Step 1: In (i) every value is shown individually — ungrouped.

Step 2: In (ii) the books are counted inside price INTERVALS — the data is arranged in groups.

Answer: Table (ii) is grouped data; table (i) is ungrouped data.

mcqs.q: Data is defined as:
options: A set of information and facts
mcqs.why: The book's definition: data is a set of information and facts; the numerical facts we get in daily life are called data.

mcqs.q: Ungrouped data is:
options: Data shown in a pie graph
Data shown individually in its original (raw) form
mcqs.why: Ungrouped data keeps every value separately, exactly as collected — like the list of 12 students' marks in Exercise 13.1, Q3(i).

mcqs.q: Raza's book-store table (price interval 512–611 → 8 books, 612–711 → 5 books, ...) is:
mcqs.why: The books are counted within price intervals (groups), so this is grouped data.

mcqs.q: A cricket team's scores listed player by player (62, 41, 15, 59, ...) form:
mcqs.why: Each player's score is shown individually in its original form — ungrouped data (Exercise 13.1, Q3(iv)).

mcqs.q: The Sindh Museum visitors table (interval 150–199 → 3 weeks, 200–249 → 4 weeks, ...) is:
mcqs.why: Visitors are counted inside intervals 150–199, 200–249, etc. — data arranged in groups is grouped data.

mcqs.q: In tally marks, the fifth mark is drawn:
mcqs.why: After every fourth mark, the fifth is drawn diagonally across them, making a bundle of five that can be counted quickly (Practical Work, Unit 13).

mcqs.q: A bundle of tally marks with the diagonal fifth mark stands for:
mcqs.why: Four straight marks plus the diagonal fifth make one bundle = 5 items.

mcqs.q: To collect the birth months of a class (Practical Work), for each student we:
options: Put one tally mark in the row of their birth month
mcqs.why: Method from the book: ask each student, add one tally mark in that month's row, bundle every five, then count each row and write the number of students.

mcqs.q: Which of these is grouped data?
mcqs.why: Only the price-interval table arranges data into groups. The others show values individually — ungrouped.

mcqs.q: The main advantage of grouping data is:
options: It makes large amounts of data easy to read and understand
It removes the need to count
mcqs.why: Grouping arranges many individual values into a few intervals, so patterns (like which price range has most books) can be seen at a glance.

lessons.title: Exercise 13.2 — Bar Graphs and Pie Graphs
lessons.notes_html:
Bar graph

A bar graph shows data with rectangular bars of the same width; the LENGTH (or height) of each bar shows the value. Bars may be vertical or horizontal. The longest bar = the greatest value.

Pie graph

A pie graph is a CIRCLE divided into sectors; the biggest sector shows the greatest share. In the games pie graph, cricket's sector is the largest (most students) and tennis's the smallest.

Worked example (from Practical Work, Unit 13)

Games bar graph data: Hockey 36, Cricket 43, Badminton 16, Football 20, Volleyball 8, Basketball 12, Boxing 1. Write a sentence from the graph.

Step 1: The greatest value is cricket, 43 — so cricket's bar is the longest (86 small squares in the book's graph).

Step 2: The smallest value is boxing, only 1 student — its bar is the shortest.

Answer: "Cricket is played by the most students, and boxing by the fewest — only 1 student."

mcqs.q: In the games bar graph (Hockey 36, Cricket 43, Badminton 16, Football 20, Volleyball 8, Basketball 12, Boxing 1), the longest bar is:
mcqs.why: Cricket has the greatest value, 43 students, so its bar is the longest — the book's own example sentence.

mcqs.q: In the same graph, the shortest bar is:
mcqs.why: Boxing is played by only 1 student — the smallest value — so its bar is the shortest.

mcqs.q: A shopkeeper's fan sales: Jan 70, Feb 50, Mar 35, Apr 60, May 90, Jun 95 (Exercise 13.2, Q1). In the vertical bar graph, the tallest bar is for:
mcqs.why: June has the highest sales, 95 fans, so June's bar is the tallest.

mcqs.q: Akbar's expenses: food 6000, education 5000, rent 4500, telephone 1500, electricity 2000, gas 300 (Exercise 13.2, Q2). The longest bar in the bar graph shows:
mcqs.why: Food, Rs 6,000, is the biggest expense, so its bar is the longest; gas (Rs 300) gives the shortest bar.

mcqs.q: Variety-show tickets: Hyderabad 10,000, Sukkur 6,000, Larkano 3,000, Dado 9,000 (Exercise 13.2, Q3). The city with the FEWEST tickets sold is:
mcqs.why: Larkano sold 3,000 tickets — fewer than Sukkur (6,000), Dado (9,000) and Hyderabad (10,000).

mcqs.q: Amjad's result: Math 90, Sindhi 80, Islamiyat 70, Urdu 65, English 60, Science 55, Social Studies 45 (Exercise 13.2, Q4). His highest bar is for:
mcqs.why: Math has the most marks (90), so in the horizontal bar graph Math's bar is the longest.

mcqs.q: In the pie graph of Class VI students' games (Exercise 13.2, Q5), the game played by the MOST students is:
mcqs.why: Cricket's sector is the largest in the pie graph — read from the sizes of the sectors, since no numbers are printed on it.

mcqs.q: In the same pie graph, the two games with EQUAL numbers of students are:
mcqs.why: In the pie graph, the sectors of football and tennis appear equal in size, so an equal number of students took part in these two games (Exercise 13.2, Q5(iii)).

mcqs.q: In the pie graph of Aftab's marks (Exercise 13.2, Q6), Aftab got the most marks in ______ and the fewest in ______:
mcqs.why: Math's sector is the largest (most marks) and English's the smallest (fewest marks); Math's sector is also slightly larger than Science's.

mcqs.q: In the attendance pie graph (Exercise 13.2, Q7), the class with the highest attendance is ______ and the lowest is ______:
mcqs.why: Class II's sector is the largest (highest attendance) and Class I's the smallest (lowest); Classes IV and V have equal sectors.

lessons.title: Review Exercise 13 — Data Handling: Mixed Practice
lessons.notes_html:
The unit in short

  • Data = a set of information and facts; numerical facts of daily life are data.
  • Ungrouped = individual/raw; grouped = arranged in intervals.
  • Pictograph: data shown as pictures — values are found by COUNTING the pictures.
  • Bar graph: equal-width rectangular bars, vertical or horizontal; longer bar = greater value. Bar graphs show data more easily and usefully than pictographs.
  • Pie graph: a circle in sectors — NOT a rectangle.

Worked example (from Review Exercise 13, Q1)

Saira's marks bar graph: Sindhi 50, Urdu 50, English 60, Science 70, Social Studies 40, Islamiyat 78, Math 80. In which subject did she get the most marks, and the fewest?

Step 1: The longest bar is Math — 80 marks.

Step 2: The shortest bar is Social Studies — 40 marks.

Step 3: Equal bars: Sindhi and Urdu, 50 marks each.

Answer: Most in Math (80), fewest in Social Studies (40).

mcqs.q: Saira got equal marks in which two subjects? (Review Q1)

mcqs.q: 'From a pictograph, numerical data can be obtained by counting the pictures.' This statement is:
mcqs.why: A pictograph shows values through pictures/symbols; counting them (with the key) gives the numbers. (Review Exercise 13, Q2(i).)

mcqs.q: 'In a bar graph, the bars have the same width.' This statement is:
mcqs.why: All bars in a bar graph are drawn with equal width; only their lengths/heights change with the values. (Review Q2(ii).)

mcqs.q: 'A rectangular shape is called a pie graph.' This statement is:
options: False — a pie graph is a circle divided into sectors
mcqs.why: A pie graph is circular — a circle cut into sectors. A rectangle belongs to bar graphs, not pie graphs. (Review Q2(iv).)

mcqs.q: Showing numerical data in the form of pictures is called a ______ graph (Review Q3).
mcqs.why: Data shown through pictures is a pictograph — the first fill-in of Review Exercise 13, Q3.

mcqs.q: Showing data with ______ graphs is much easier and more useful than with a pictograph (Review Q3).
mcqs.why: The book's fill-in answer is 'bar': bar graphs present data more easily and usefully than pictographs.

mcqs.q: In a bar graph, the bars are in ______ form or ______ form (Review Q3).
mcqs.why: Bars may stand vertically (columns) or lie horizontally — the two forms used in Exercise 13.2, Q1–Q4.

mcqs.q: ______ is defined as a set of information and facts (Review Q3).
mcqs.why: Data is defined as a set of information and facts — the same definition as Exercise 13.1, Q1.

mcqs.q: In the pie graph of 600 Hajj pilgrims (Practical Work), the greatest in number are:
mcqs.why: The men's sector is the largest in the pie graph, so men are the greatest in number; children are the least, and the children are NOT equal to the women.

mcqs.q: The length of cricket's bar in the book's games bar graph is 86 small squares for 43 students. This shows that in a bar graph:
options: Each small square stands for 1 student
The bar length is proportional to the value (2 squares per student here)
mcqs.why: 43 students ↔ 86 squares means the length grows in proportion to the value — 2 small squares per student on this graph's scale. Reading a bar graph always uses its scale.
